paras: In late July 1881, Black laborers hired to build the Louisville, New Albany and St. Louis railroad in Crawford County, Indiana, were threatened with exclusion from the county, and local officials refused to protect them. Reports differed on whether construction halted or the men went to work, but no violence was reported. Papers in Indianapolis, Chicago, Memphis and Savannah carried the story, the Indianapolis Leader calling it "a gross outrage" in a state "north of the Ohio river."

Contractors on the new line, called the St. Louis Air-Line, engaged Black laborers after failing to obtain white workers, according to an Indianapolis dispatch to the Cincinnati Enquirer. The same dispatch described Crawford County as a river county with no railroad and a single Black resident, an elderly blind man named Archie Boone.

According to a special dispatch to the Times from Leavenworth, "certain disorderly roughs" asserted that Black laborers would not be allowed into the county to work on the road. The contractors went to Leavenworth to ask county officials for protection and were told that the laborers would indeed not be allowed in and that no protection could be given. The Enquirer account placed the refusal with the Sheriff, who said he would not be responsible for the result if Black laborers were brought in.

The Times dispatch reported that railroad building was "stopped for the present." A day later, however, Charles I. Benham of Crawford County told the Enquirer that the contractor, Serples, had taken his men in despite the threats and had 200 Black laborers at work, with no trouble so far.

A paragraph printed in Memphis on August 12 said the laborers had "fared not at all well" because of local hostility and that trouble was expected, but it gave no particulars. No report of violence, arrests or action by the governor appears in the coverage.

The Indianapolis Leader ran the story as an editorial headed "NO NEGROES WANTED," urging Governor Porter to protect laborers "white or black" and calling for federal authorities if the state did nothing. The Chicago Daily Tribune reprinted the Enquirer dispatch under a "Negrophobia" headline that mocked the county's "ignorant populace" while itself calling the workers "dusky laborers" and "harmless Hamites." The short paragraph in the Memphis Daily Appeal and the Savannah Morning News reported the hostility without comment, calling the men "dusky laborers" and "darkies."

The accounts conflict on whether work stopped: the Times dispatch said it did, while the later Enquirer dispatch, citing a named county resident, said 200 men were at work. They also differ on the officials' stance, with the Times having them endorse the exclusion and the Enquirer recording only the Sheriff's refusal of responsibility.

reader.title: Threats against Black railroad laborers in Crawford County, Indiana
bases: Black railroad laborers were threatened with exclusion from the county and officials refused them protection, but no violence was reported (A2, A3, A5).

Two separate dispatches, one to the Times from Leavenworth (A2) and one from Indianapolis to the Cincinnati Enquirer (A3), agree that Black laborers were threatened and that county authorities refused protection, though they differ on whether work stopped.

accounts.label: Times dispatch from Leavenworth (via Indianapolis Leader)
accounts.gist: Roughs said Black laborers would not be allowed in; county officials agreed and refused protection, and railroad building stopped.

accounts.label: Enquirer dispatch from Indianapolis, citing Charles I. Benham
accounts.gist: The Sheriff refused responsibility, but contractor Serples took his laborers in anyway and had 200 at work with no trouble yet.

accounts.label: Later news paragraph
accounts.gist: The laborers had fared badly because of local hostility; the Sheriff refused protection and trouble was expected.

framing.detail: The Indianapolis Leader headlined it 'NO NEGROES WANTED' and called it 'a gross outrage', demanding state or federal protection.
The Chicago Tribune's 'Negrophobia' piece mocked the county's prejudice while calling the laborers 'dusky' and 'harmless Hamites'.
The Memphis and Savannah paragraphs reported the hostility as news, calling the men 'dusky laborers' and 'darkies'.
